div.head: LECTURE XXI.

head.hi: And Israel said unto Joseph, I had not though so see thy face; and, lo! God hath showed me also thy seed.

div.p:
THE internal evidence of the truth of the Old as well as the New Testament, is by much too considerable to be overlooked. By internal evidence, of course, I mean those marks of reality and genuineness, which are produced by the probability, fitness, pertinence, connexion both of the speeches and actions therein occurring, and which are accommodated to the personages, the times in which they lived, the habits of their life, the circumstances which controlled, the motives which influenced them, in such a manner as no human invention has ever equalled, and no alteration could improve. Whoever is desirous of discovering, and capable of appreciating these marks of reality, these internal proofs of truth stamped on the Scriptures, no doubt, by the will and pmport of God who g-iveth us largely every method of improving our
faith, will find them no where more thickly sown than in the five concluding chapters of the book of Genesis. The collected wisdom of this world has not furnished in any other writings such an impressive description of every human feeling, whether it be of envy, cruelty, grief, resignation, gratitude, pardon, or piety, all working out one great scheme of good.

When it was related to Jacob, that his favourite son, whom he had so long and deeply deplored, that Joseph was yet alive, the workings of his mind are represented with a brevity, force, and truth, shaming the most laboured efforts of other ancient historians. Let me place the very words before you: "Jacob's heart fainted, for he believed them not."—This disbelief was not a disbelief in the power of God, but proceeded from a proper sense of his own unworthiness. What had he done to receive such great reward? Why should the Lord turn his sorrow into joy like the rivers of the south? He was therefore like one who did dream; he had not dared to hope that he should ever see all his children's children and peace upon Israel. Of the same nature was the pious doubt which overwhelmed the faculties of the disciples (when their crucified Redeemer reappeared among them), while they believed not for joy. Anon, however, when his sons had repeatedrepeat-
ed to him their wonderful tidings, and confirmed their truth by showing the presents of which themselves were bearers, then the spirit of Jacob their father revived; and Israel said, " It is enough; Joseph my son is yet alive: I will go and see him before I die."

Prosperity of any sort is a great trial of the heart, and indeed a very accurate test in general, whether it be well with God. The gift does not always remind us of the Giver. When we are magnified by any sudden visitation of good, be it ours to magnify the Lord; and when our spirit revives from the conflict of doubt, and swells into joy, let it habitually rejoice in the Lord our Saviour. Adversity seldom fails to cast us on our knees; for, when human friends forsake or look cool, the heart in very bitterness, as well as destitution, seeketh for a heavenly friend. But as Solomon says to those of immature years, "Remember thy Creator in the days of thy youth;" so docs the law of the Gospel, which is greater than Solomon, say unto all, Remember thy Creator in the day of rejoicing, lest your triumph be made a snare unto you. Jacob did remember the Lord with his whole heart at this most critical moment. He did not venture to indulge even what appeared to be the natural fondness of a parent, without mixing with it a truly pious feeling.
Having prepared all for his journey, he did not presume to commence it without an appeal to God, evidently trusting, that in a measure of such importance as the quitting Canaan, he should not fail to receive heavenly direction. He offered sacrifices at Beer-sheba, unto the God of his father Isaac: he selected Beer-sheba, no doubt, because there it was that his father had sacrificed, and there had received communications from the Most High.

Jacob might well suppose, that if his projected journey was displeasing to God, he should not be suffered to proceed. From the answer which he received, it is most clear that Jacob had some such apprehensions. God spake unto him in the visions of the night, as he had spoken in old time unto Laban, previous to their most remarkable reconciliation, on which Jacob's progress into Canaan depended. "I am God, the God of thy father: fear not to go down into Egypt; for I will make of thee a great nation. I will go down with thee into Egypt, and I will also surely bring thee up again; and Joseph shall put his hand upon thine eyes."—The peremptory terms of this prophetical promise could not but encourage Jacob to quit Canaan for Egypt. The blessings held out were abundantly realized in the fourth generation. But some of the words of the Lord were also doubly
fulfilled: "I will go down with thee into Egypt, and I will also assuredly bring thee up again." This met its most important completion, when our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ was convey- ed by Joseph and Mary, warned in a dream, into Egypt, to avoid the cruelty of Herod, and afterwards returned to be made the head of all nations, even of the Christian world, to which also the prophecy of Hosea beareth witness, saying, " Out of Egypt have I called my son." Accordingly Jacob went into Egypt, and all his seed with him. It is mentioned, that all his seed went with him, that we might be sure of their having left none in the land of Canaan, who might afterwards have openly or secretly aided them in their conquest of it, which would so far have impugned the miraculous interfer- ence of the Almighty, who brought them in with a mighty hand, and cast out the inhabitants before them.

The number of Israelites, including Joseph and his two sons, were seventy: these seventy, in the course of about two hundred years, became two millions; an augmentation unexampled under the most favourable circumstances, but undeniably miraculous, if we consider that the Israelites lived apart from the Egyptians, were devoted to pastoral employments, intermarried with their own families only,
received no accession of numbers from the intercourse of commerce nor incorporation of strangers, were soon reduced by the Egyptians to a species of servitude of all states least friendly to increase of numbers, and were finally, for a time, visited by that dreadful order which a Pharaoh, knowing not Joseph, issued for the destruction of the male children; but which order could no more extend its influence over Moses, than the similar order of Herod could extend to the life of Christ, whom Moses foretold and typified.

After a sojournment of seventeen years in Egypt, Jacob was sensible of the approach of death. He made, accordingly, all the dispositions which might be expected from an affectionate father and a confident believer in the promises of God. Before he called about him his other children, he summoned to his presence Joseph, whose unfailing filial affection gave sure pledge that no injunction of a dying parent would fall to the ground unheeded. From Joseph he exacted a promise, that his body should not lie in Egypt, but be interred in the sepulchre of his fathers. As it can be really of no consequence where the mortal body moulders, this injunction of Jacob's was doubtless intended to keep alive in the minds of his descendants the promises of God, that
they should in due time return to the land of Canaan. He next pronounced a peculiar blessing on Joseph and the two sons of Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh, elevating them to a parity of inheritance with his own children; prophesying, that they should be the heads of two of the twelve tribes, and predicting that Ephraim, the youngest, should be the more powerful of the two. This was afterwards so decidedly the case, that Ephraim is often sub- stituted in the prophecies for the whole kingdom of Israel, i.e. one tribe for ten. It may here also be proper to observe, that as the tribe of Levi was entirely consecrated to the priesthood, the double representation thus assigned to Joseph in the persons of his two sons, a reward, doubtless, for his superior discharge of every duty, served but to complete the number of the efficient tribes to twelve. The last words which Jacob spoke on this occasion were replete with prophecy: "Behold, I die; but God shall be with you, and bring you again unto the land of your fathers." The light of faith and inspiration seems, in this and several other instances, to burn more bright and strong as the spirit of the man was drawing nearer and nearer to the God who gave it.

In the same elevated, but more figurative manner, did he open to all his sons the epitome
of their future destiny; highly appropriate, and wonderfully accurate, as far as the remnant of history allows us to pronounce. But he was most explicit with regard to that which should befall Judah in the latter days; and in that are we most interested. The whole of this prophecy occupies the text, from the 5th to the 12th verse inclusive. Every word of it deserves repeated perusal, and is intimately connected with the effusions of Isaiah and all the prophets. But the words of the 10th verse I shall now remind you of—"The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, till Shiloh come; and to him shall the gathering of the people be." All the learned in Jewish history agree, that by Shiloh was meant that Messiah whom we acknowledge in Jesus Christ. The Jews, who were the remnant of Judah, had a king, had laws, till after the coming, the death, the resurrection of our Sa- viour, the formation of his church, and the adoption of the name of Christian. The Jews, descendants of Judah, had a king and laws, though all the other tribes had lost such marks of national existence. When forty years had elapsed from the beginning of Christ's ministry, the descendants of Judah, also, lost this their surviving relic of distinction: the sceptre departed from Judah, and the lawgiver from between his feet. Such a fulfilment of Jacob's
words in the dispersion of the Jews, whilst it fills us with assurance and faith in the Gospel, must also prepare us to expect the final accomplishment of all things, at the second coming of the Lord: "for to him shall the gathering of the people be."

Joseph most faithfully performed his father's command—he buried him in the sepulchre of Abraham; thus completing the perfect character of a son, in whom was found no speck of disobedience. His faultlessness as a brother was yet to shine forth with additional lustre. As guilt is always cowardly, the fears of his brethren were now again excited, lest he should requite them with evil for what they had done unto him. What did Joseph say in reply to their abject humiliation? "Fear not, for I am in the place of God: but as for you, ye thought evil against me, but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive." Is not this a prediction of the character which our Saviour should assume; of his being in the place of God, of his ministry among those who should think evil against him; of his coming according to the foreknowledge and predetermined counsel of the Most High to save much people alive? Is it not so, my beloved friends, at this day? Well might Pharaoh say, "Can we find such a man
as this is a man in whom the spirit of God is? This spirit failed not Joseph during his life. We read in the close of the book of Genesis, that the children of his grandsons were brought up on his knees: in spite of all the avocations of public duty and the privileges of high rank, he found time to instruct even the fourth generation of his family in the worship of the true God. This was the more necessary, because, through the connexions of Asenath his wife, who was the daughter of the priest of On, they might have been insensibly led to embrace the religion of Egypt, and thus have forfeited the inheritance with their fellow Israelites in Canaan.

Thus was the whole eventful life of Joseph marked by a scrupulous adherence to his duty, and an enduring faith in the merciful protection of God. He died as he had lived: for, as the Apostle St. Paul saith, " By faith Joseph, when he died, made mention of the departing of the children of Israel, and gave commandment concerning his bones." With those words of the sacred historian, to which the Apostle refers, and with which he concludes the book of Ge- nesis, I shall conclude my remarks upon it. "And Joseph said unto his brethren, I die: and God will surely visit you, and bring you out of this land unto the land which he sware to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob. And Joseph
took an oath of the children of Israel, saying, God will surely visit you, and ye shall carry up my bones from hence. So Joseph died, being an hundred and ten years old: and they embalmed him, and he was put in a cofin in Egypt."

We have thus the evidence of an Apostle, that the book of Genesis contains what it did contain eighteen hundred years ago: proof enough, were there none else, of its genuineness. It is, separately considered, the most important of all the books of the Old Testament. I have briefly touched on its most striking parts in twenty-one discourses; but were we to discourse or write till the subject seemed to be exhausted, we might say with the beloved disciple, "There are also many other things, the which, if they should be written every one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written." I therefore conjure and exhort you to be familiar with it; it will produce a desire of searching into other parts of Scripture, and supply the best means of unfolding its subsequent mysteries. It is the first link of that chain which joins earth to heaven: it is the clue of that thread, which in the hands of the humble and meek, shall lead them through the valley of the shadow of death, to a knowledge of the truth in Christ, which is the perfect day.
